title: type2_recall is blind: the only curated Type-2 recall check passes with the curated duplicate deleted
body:
## The defect

[`crates/deslop-test-support/src/corpus_confidence.rs:357`](https://github.com/Nimblesite/Deslop/blob/main/crates/deslop-test-support/src/corpus_confidence.rs#L357) — `check_one_curated_type2` — is the only assertion guarding Type-2 rename recall on real-repository ground truth. Both of its clauses ask the same weak question: *does **some** cluster touch these two paths?*

```rust
if !reports_clone_spanning(report, &files) {          // :360 — any cluster, any extent
    …"no cluster spans {files:?}"…
}
let vouched = visible_clusters(report)                // :367
    .iter()
    .any(|cluster| gate_vouched(cluster) && cluster_shows_span(cluster, &files));  // :369
```

`reports_clone_spanning` ([`corpus.rs:541`](https://github.com/Nimblesite/Deslop/blob/main/crates/deslop-test-support/src/corpus.rs#L541)) and `cluster_shows_span` ([`corpus.rs:591`](https://github.com/Nimblesite/Deslop/blob/main/crates/deslop-test-support/src/corpus.rs#L591)) are pure path-set membership. Neither reads the cluster's extent, node count, size or rank. So the check cannot distinguish **"reported as one module"** from **"reported as a buried fragment"** from **"not reported at all, but the two files happen to share a five-line accessor"** — the three outcomes its own doc comment names as the failures it exists to catch.

`corpus/tokio.json` curates the pair as *"the two standard-stream handles are one module written twice"* — 134 and 183 lines, every declaration and impl header renamed. Both witnesses below satisfy the check while that claim is false.

## Witness 1 — the check passes with the curated duplicate deleted

Scan of the pinned `tokio-1.49.0` clone at `7bb29d4`, with the curated module cluster removed from the rendered report and both clauses re-applied:

```
clusters after deleting the curated module pair: 2396 of 2397
clause 1 reports_clone_spanning: True
clause 2 shown gate-vouched    : True
  -> satisfied by rank 56 nearly_identical size=17 nodes=31 rc=0.62
     unrelated files it also spans: 11, e.g. tokio/src/io/stdin.rs,
     tokio/src/net/tcp/listener.rs, tokio/src/net/tcp/stream.rs
```

The survivor is a 31-node `fn as_raw_fd(&self) -> RawFd { std::io::stdout().as_raw_fd() }` accessor family with 17 occurrences across `net/tcp/`, `net/udp.rs`, `net/unix/`, `net/windows/` and `process/unix/`. Five lines of platform boilerplate stand in as proof of a 134-line module rename. **Delete the ground truth entirely and `type2_recall` still reports green.**

## Witness 2 — the check passed while the finding was unreachable

At `7332719` (parent of the `[PIPELINE-CLUSTER-ELECT]` weld fix) the same scan reports the pair, but as a **39-node fragment at rank 1628 of 2155**:

```
7332719  clusters=2155 dup=29.2%
  module: rank 1628  nearly_identical  size=2  nodes=39
          tokio/src/io/stderr.rs:10-78   tokio/src/io/stdout.rs:9-127
```

One commit later it is the 395-node whole-module view at rank 78. `type2_recall` is green on both. Ranking is the product — a finding at rank 1628 is a finding the user does not get — and the gate reports no difference between the two.

## Why this matters beyond the check itself

**It is the recall-side twin of #401.** That issue establishes the same defect for the only curated *precision* surface (`check_boilerplate_not_ranked_first` matching raw source text, unsound in both directions). Both are the one instrument asserting their property on a real repository, and both can answer wrong.

**A red `type2_recall` is not trustworthy either.** #428 reports this check firing on this exact pair. Ten rebuilt commits spanning 21–23 Aug — including the reporter's own build, identified by its `2409 clusters / 30.6125%` against the reported `2410 / 30.6%` — all report the pair as a shown, gate-vouched `nearly_identical` cluster, and two identical scans of that build produce byte-identical payloads. The check that raised #428 is one whose green cannot be believed and whose red was not reproducible from any committed state.

**It is also unrun.** Per #422 the corpus suite is `#[ignore]`d out of the PR gate, so nothing in CI exercises this assertion at all. Weak *and* dormant.

**The plan grades it sound.** [`docs/plans/corpus-assertion.md:86`](https://github.com/Nimblesite/Deslop/blob/main/docs/plans/corpus-assertion.md#L86):

| check id | asserts | today |
|---|---|---|
| `type2_recall` | curated renames reported, gate-vouched, shown | ✅ |

L5 of the same document says of `check_recall`: *"asserts only that **some** cluster spans the curated paths"* — and contrasts it favourably against the Type-2 check. That argument applies verbatim to `type2_recall`, which also asks only that. Code and plan disagree; per `AGENTS.md` that is a stop-and-report, so the table is left as-is pending this issue.

## Fix

- [ ] Failing test first, in [`corpus_confidence/tests/curated.rs`](https://github.com/Nimblesite/Deslop/blob/main/crates/deslop-test-support/src/corpus_confidence/tests/curated.rs): a report whose curated pair is **absent** but where a wide boilerplate family spans both curated paths must raise `type2_recall`. Watch it fail for the real reason — today the check passes. A second case for Witness 2: a spanning cluster far below the curated extent must also fail.
- [ ] Give `must_find_type2` entries a curated **extent** — minimum node count or line span — so the assertion pins *the module*, not any cluster touching two paths. The tokio entry's `verified` field already states the extent in prose; make it machine-checked.
- [ ] Apply `max_rank` to `must_find_type2` as `check_curated_recall` already does for `must_find` ([`corpus_confidence.rs:280`](https://github.com/Nimblesite/Deslop/blob/main/crates/deslop-test-support/src/corpus_confidence.rs#L280)), so Witness 2 fails.
- [ ] Correct the `type2_recall` row in `docs/plans/corpus-assertion.md` and the check description in `corpus/known-failures.json`, both of which currently claim more than the code asserts.
- [ ] Re-verify #428 against the strengthened check and record the verdict there.

## Repro

```
node scripts/corpus/fetch-corpus.mjs tokio
cargo build --release --bin deslop
cargo test --release -p deslop --test corpus_repos -- --ignored --exact \
  --nocapture --test-threads=1 corpus_tokio_rust
```

Note the target name: `corpus_repos` moved back out of `suite`, so #428's `--test suite … corpus_repos::corpus_tokio_rust` now matches nothing and reports `0 tests, 454 filtered out`.

## Context

Found while investigating #428. Same class as the "assertion instruments that pass vacuously" set in [`docs/plans/fused-score-followups.md`](https://github.com/Nimblesite/Deslop/blob/main/docs/plans/fused-score-followups.md) §5 — #415, #398, #412 — and this would be a fourth member.

title: Cluster ids collide: the id is the smallest member digest, so unrelated clusters that share a normalised subtree are stamped the same
body:
`cluster_id_source` in `crates/deslop-core/src/cluster.rs` derives a cluster's published id from the **smallest member digest alone**:

```rust
fn cluster_id_source(members: &[Fingerprint]) -> [u8; 32] {
    members
        .iter()
        .min_by_key(|member| member.hash)
        .map_or([0_u8; 32], |member| member.hash)
}
```

The digest is the *normalised subtree* hash, so any two clusters whose members share a normalised subtree are stamped with the same id, no matter which files they occupy.

## Reproduction

```
deslop crates/deslop/tests/fixtures/python-issue-107-chained-dict-assert --min-nodes 4 --no-incremental
```

Three separate clusters are published, all stamped `bc8ca6ce6565ba6d`:

| id | occurrences |
|---|---|
| `bc8ca6ce6565ba6d` | `test_configs_patch.py` L6, `test_configs_patch.py` L7 |
| `bc8ca6ce6565ba6d` | `test_sandbox_coverage.py` L6, `test_sandbox_coverage.py` L7 |
| `bc8ca6ce6565ba6d` | `test_openapi.py` L6, `test_openapi.py` L7 |

Each is the repeated `data["model_config"]` subscript chain in a different, unrelated pytest module. Their normalised subtrees are equal, so their ids are equal.

## Why this is an accuracy defect, not cosmetics

- **`cluster-by-id` and the editor cannot address two thirds of these findings.** The id is the handle the MCP lookup, the VSIX selection, and "go to cluster" all resolve. Whichever cluster is found first answers for all of them.
- **The ranking tie-break stops being a total order.** `[PIPELINE-RANK-WORST-FIRST]` sorts by weight descending, "ties broken by cluster id so the order is total and reproducible". Equal weights *and* equal ids leave the order unpinned, which contradicts `[PIPELINE-DETERMINISM]`.
- **Counting distinct ids under-counts findings.** Any consumer deduplicating on id silently drops real clusters.

## Pinned by

`crates/deslop/tests/cluster_id_uniqueness.rs::no_two_published_clusters_share_one_id` — currently red, and red for this reason.

## Note on the fix

The id has to stay derived from content so it survives a file move, but it must also distinguish two findings that merely share a shape. Mixing the members' workspace-relative paths into the digest does both. Every committed cluster id moves when it lands, so it wants to be sequenced with the other normalisation re-cuts rather than dropped into the middle of them.

title: SHOWSTOPPER: Deslop cannot analyse flutter/flutter — killed at 30 min with no report, requirement is 600 s
body:
## TL;DR

Deslop cannot finish scanning the Flutter codebase. A full scan was killed after 30 minutes with no report produced at all — the target is under 10 minutes. Memory use also reached 14.6 GB, more than double its 7 GB limit. A tool that can't get through a mainstream open-source repo in ten minutes isn't usable on the codebases it's meant for. This is a showstopper.

## Details

A complete, from-scratch scan of flutter/flutter (6,231 files) was run with every optional feature turned off. It never finished. Roughly what happens:

- Finding the files takes 1 second.
- Reading and fingerprinting them all takes about 15.5 minutes — already past the 10-minute target before any comparison starts.
- The comparison stage then generates 55 million candidate pairs, and the step that verifies them had run for 13+ minutes and was nowhere near done when the run was killed at the 30-minute mark.
- No report of any kind was written.
- Peak memory: 14.6 GB (the limit for this corpus is 7 GB), reached before clustering even starts.
- Despite running on a 24-core machine, the whole pipeline uses one core.

Two separate problems, each fatal on its own: the reading/fingerprinting stage is too slow, and the pair-verification step never completes. The second is proven to be new — a feature added recently made it dramatically slower; the first is suspected but not yet proven (details and caveats in the AI section).

Along the way this also exposed: debug logging that floods 72 MB while diagnosing the very stage being measured; no progress output for 15 minutes straight, so a slow run is indistinguishable from a hang; and memory that grows without bound because everything found so far is kept in RAM.

An earlier scan of the same repo (issue #166) did complete — 9.6 GB, ~10 minutes. This one doesn't finish at all, so the regression is real.

## Steps To Reproduce

Expect to kill it manually — it will not finish:

1. Clone the corpus:

   ```
   git clone https://github.com/flutter/flutter && cd flutter
   ```

   (3.38.9 @ `67323de285b00232883f53b84095eb72be97d35c` — 6,231 files.)

2. Run the scan with extras off:

   ```
   deslop . --no-incremental --embeddings off --no-fail-over --notext --nohtml --output /tmp/deslop
   ```

3. Watch: file discovery completes in ~1s, then nothing for ~15 minutes (fingerprinting), then candidate-pair comparison starts and grinds. At 30 minutes there is still no report file.
4. Kill it. Note peak memory (14.6 GB observed).

## Details (for AI)

```shell
# environment
binary: release build from 44dba6d
corpus: flutter/flutter 3.38.9 @ 67323de285b00232883f53b84095eb72be97d35c — 6,231 files (6,153 Dart, 56 Python, 21 JS, 1 TS)
flags: --no-incremental --embeddings off --no-fail-over --notext --nohtml
machine: 24 logical cores; cpu/wall = 0.983 (whole pipeline is one core)

# measured timeline (seconds)
1.2      discovery complete — 6,231 files
929.1    fingerprint corpus built — 3,466,996 fingerprints / signatures
954.2    LSH complete — 55,332,661 candidate pairs (LSH itself 21.9s)
1019.9   first shared-subtree rescue overlap measured
1801.6   last rescue overlap — 793,076 measurements, rescue incomplete
1801.7   killed. No report.
peak rss: 14,624.9 MB (ceiling 7,168 MB — 2.04x, reached pre-clustering)

# failure 1 — corpus + signature build ~928s
6.7 files/s, ~3.7k signatures/s, one file at a time; log event `fingerprint corpus built` covers parse + normalize + structural fingerprints + sibling-window fingerprints + token-range resolution + MinHash — no internal timing boundaries, so tree-sitter's share is unknown
hypothesis (unproven): crates/deslop-core/src/pipeline/signatures.rs:56 now routes every known-language fingerprint through token_stream_for_fingerprint_with_language (crates/deslop-core/src/tokens.rs#L55); at f92300e the resolver ran only for Python / known-boilerplate ranges, everything else took the cheap exact-node path; synthetic sibling windows now trigger full root-range token resolution + allocation + MinHash across millions of fingerprints, and formerly offset-scoped signatures can collide on real token content — feeding the 55M pair explosion. Log lacks exact-node vs sibling-window and token-derived vs fallback counts.

# failure 2 — shared-subtree rescue never finishes (demonstrated post-f92300e)
apply_shared_subtree_rescue (crates/deslop-core/src/overlap.rs#L79), called from crates/deslop-core/src/pipeline/session/render.rs#L78: sequential walk of the 55.3M-pair candidate slice, Zhang-Shasha tree edit distance O(n^2*d^2) at the 768-node cap on every eligible pair; 793,076 measurements before the kill; never reaches `shared-subtree rescue overlaps measured` or `clustering by transitive closure`

# exposed observability gaps
measure_onto debug logging: one record per overlap measurement — 793,076 records / 72 MB by the 504k mark
no bounded progress reporting between 1.2s and 929s — slow indistinguishable from hung
memory: unbounded bulk retention (sources + normalized trees + fingerprints + signatures resident; pair vector, candidate objects, endpoint views, pair-result caches on top)

# relations and targets
requirement: complete flutter/flutter analysis < 600s; peak rss <= 7,168 MiB
manifest ceiling: corpus/flutter.json max_wall_seconds: 900 — needs to come down to 600 once the scan completes
related: #166 (completed run: 9.56 GB / 584 s), #414 (corpus_flutter_dart [CORPUS-CEILINGS] breach: 1014.7 s / 10,177 MB, hidden by --skip corpus_)
forensics: docs/plans/flutter-analyzer-performance-report.md [PERF-FLUTTER-TODO] — itemised breakdown (measurement, corpus build, pair amplification, rescue, memory, observability, accuracy protection, gate, docs)

# evidence caveat
no exact f92300e->HEAD attribution: debug run killed; info-level run stopped mid-corpus-build ~725s; f92300e comparison contaminated by concurrent build + second analyser; code compared against moving HEAD. Controlled A/B with aggregate counters still needed. Proven: current revision does not finish; shared-subtree rescue is new serial cost post-f92300e.
```

## Acceptance Criteria (for AI)

- [ ] Cold, non-incremental `flutter/flutter` analysis **completes in < 600 s**
- [ ] Peak RSS **≤ 7,168 MiB**
- [ ] Every stage runs — clustering, ranking, rendering — and the JSON report plus all requested formats are produced
- [ ] Every curated Flutter `must_find` result preserved; no new false positives or false negatives
- [ ] Deterministic output across repeated cold runs
- [ ] The gate is executable and fails on breach, measured against the release artifact users receive
- [ ] Diagnostic logging stays bounded and useful for the full Flutter workload

## Screenshots

None.

title: Curate [CORPUS-SCOPE] bounds for flutter and fsharp
body:
## What is unfinished

`[CORPUS-SCOPE]` requires every `corpus/*.json` manifest to carry `expect_files_min` and `expect_clusters`. Seven of nine now do, measured against the release binary at the pinned shas. `flutter.json` and `fsharp.json` do not.

## Why they are not curated

Curating a bound means measuring it, and those two repositories are the ones the corpus suite already refuses to run in CI. Both are recorded in `corpus/known-failures.json` under the `memory` check: they exceed the 7168 MB ceiling, which is the RAM of a standard GitHub Actions runner (#166). A local measurement pass reached 7.5 GB peak RSS on fsharp and was still climbing at eleven minutes; flutter is the larger of the two.

Measuring a bound for a repository the gate is designed never to scan spends twenty minutes of machine time to produce a number nothing in CI will ever read.

## Consequence today

`corpus_manifest_contract.rs::every_manifest_curates_a_non_vacuous_scan_scope` fails on the two uncurated manifests. It is `#[ignore]`d citing this issue. The assertions are unchanged — no bound was relaxed and no manifest was given a placeholder number.

## Done when

Either the two manifests carry measured bounds, or `[CORPUS-SCOPE]` states that a repository excluded from the gate by a tracked resource breach declares that exclusion explicitly rather than carrying an unverifiable number. The second is likely the right answer while #166 is open: a curated bound that nothing checks asserts nothing.

Blocked on #166.

title: Go implicit interfaces are invisible to [CLONE-NOISE-POLYMORPHIC-CONTRACT], and body_shape misses selector_expression
body:
## Defect

Two gaps, one root: the polymorphic-signature suppression cannot see a Go contract.

### 1. No lexical enclosing type

`[CLONE-NOISE-POLYMORPHIC-CONTRACT]` (`crates/deslop-core/src/cluster_filters/contract_index.rs`) proves a subject method is contract-forced by resolving the *nearest enclosing type declaration* and asking whether a transitive base declares a member of that name.

Go declares methods outside the receiver type:

```go
func (s *S3Sink) RecordEntry(entry Entry) error { ... }
```

`RecordEntry` has no enclosing `type` node, and interface satisfaction is never written down, so `enclosing_container` returns `None`, the base list is empty, and the proof can never succeed. The filter therefore **fails open** on Go: two same-signature implementations of one Go interface with different bodies are never suppressed.

This is a missed suppression (a potential false positive in the report), never a false negative — the deliberate trade recorded in `docs/specs/noise.md` under `[CLONE-NOISE-POLYMORPHIC-CONTRACT]`.

### 2. `selector_expression` is not a reach kind

`crates/deslop-core/src/cluster_filters/body_shape.rs` `REACH_KINDS` lists `attribute`, `field_expression`, `member_access_expression`, `member_expression` — but not Go's `selector_expression`. So a Go body's collaborator and callee names are erased from the shape stream, and two same-shaped Go backends that reach for entirely different collaborators compare as one identical stream. That is the same defect `python_same_shape_backends.rs` pins for Python, unpinned for Go.

## Required work

- A Go strategy for implicit contracts: resolve a method's receiver type name, index the interfaces declared in the corpus, and require structural satisfaction (every method of some interface the receiver type implements) before suppressing — or state explicitly in the spec that Go is out of scope.
- Add `selector_expression` to `REACH_KINDS`, **with a fixture that fails without it**. Do not add it unpinned: widening the stream changes what every suppression considers "the same body".

## Regression pins to add

- A Go fixture with one interface and two same-signature, different-backend implementations; assert the contract pair is absent from the report.
- In the same scan, a consistently renamed Go free-function copy; assert it stays visible with exact paths, ranges, bucket, signals, files analysed, and duplicated LOC. An empty report must fail the test.

## Where it came from

Split out of the pre-merge reaudit of `worktree-fused-score-followups`, which landed the method-level contract proof for the lexical languages (`python_inherited_contract_boundary.rs`). Go was left failing open rather than shipping an unproven suppression.

title: Corpus suite cannot run in the PR gate: minutes of wall time and >13 GB peak per repository (blocked on #166)
body:
## Why this exists

`make test` no longer selects any test by name (gh #412). The one suite that still must not run in the release gate is the real-repository corpus gate, and it needs a **stated, tracked reason** rather than a silent filter.

This issue is that reason. Every `#[ignore]` on `crates/deslop/tests/corpus_repos.rs` cites it.

## The measurement

`[CORPUS-PIN]` pins nine repositories by commit. A single gate test clones the repository and scans it end to end:

- `flutter/flutter` peaks around **9.5 GB** and takes **9m44s** (#166).
- `dotnet/fsharp` and `flutter/flutter` peak above **13 GB** — past a standard GitHub-hosted runner (7 GB / 14 GB tiers).
- Wall time and peak RSS are **runner-dependent**, so `[CORPUS-CEILINGS]` cannot assert a stable budget on shared CI hardware.

A PR gate that clones nine repositories would be measured in tens of minutes and would OOM on the larger two.

## What runs instead

- `.github/workflows/corpus.yml` runs a slice sized to finish in about a minute, on a schedule, never on `pull_request` (`[CORPUS-CI]`).
- `make test-corpus` runs the full suite locally via `-- --ignored`.
- `make test` / `make ci` still **compile and lint** the target — commit `77bcbaed5` left it uncompilable because feature-gating had removed it from `--all-targets`. Gating must cost coverage of a test's execution, never of its compilation.

## The plan to lift the skip

Blocked on **#166**. Once analysis is streamed rather than held whole-corpus in RAM, peak memory should fit a hosted runner, and the per-repository tests can move into the PR gate one repository at a time — cheapest first (`tokio`, `nest`), largest last (`flutter`, `fsharp`).

Plan: `docs/plans/corpus-assertion.md` · Spec: `[CORPUS-CI]`, `[CORPUS-CEILINGS]` in `docs/specs/corpus.md`

## Definition of done

Delete the `[SKIP-TOO-LARGE-FOR-CI]` `#[ignore]` from every test in `crates/deslop/tests/corpus_repos.rs` and remove its entries from the curated set in `crates/deslop/tests/skip_policy_contract.rs`.

title: C# Identical upgrade compares only method_declaration nodes, manufacturing false 'every copy is the same' claims
body:
## The defect

`report_render.rs` upgrades a C# cluster to the `identical` bucket via a fallback, `csharp_method_declarations_are_equivalent`, when the raw slices are not byte-equivalent: it collects the `method_declaration` nodes fully contained in each member range, compares those, and **ignores every other member in the range** — properties, fields, constructors, nested types. Two ranges that differ semantically therefore render:

> Identical code. Safe to extract — every copy is the same. (Type-1 or Type-2 exact clone)

"Safe to extract" is dangerously false: extracting would erase the differing member.

## Real-repository evidence

Jellyfin corpus at the pinned v10.10.7 (`aefb9b2cffca`), cluster `3058797115ad9d45`:

- `Emby.Server.Implementations/Sorting/DateLastMediaAddedComparer.cs:20-49`
- `Emby.Server.Implementations/Sorting/DatePlayedComparer.cs:22-51`

The two ranges are identical **except** `public ItemSortBy Type => ItemSortBy.DateLastContentAdded;` vs `ItemSortBy.DatePlayed;` — a semantic property difference — yet the report claims `identical` with the every-copy-is-the-same interpretation. Hand-verified by extracting both byte ranges and diffing: 1 changed line of 30. Several further jellyfin `identical` clusters show the same shape (e.g. `ItemsController` vs `TrailersController`, ranges of different lengths labelled identical).

## What was done (strict accuracy rule)

1. **Failing test, watched failing for the real reason**: `crates/deslop/tests/csharp_identical_overclaim.rs` with fixture `csharp-identical-overclaim` (two classes, byte-identical methods, differing `Kind` property — the jellyfin comparer shape). It asserts the [CLONE-BUCKETS-IDENTICAL] contract black-box: every rendered `identical` cluster's slices must be equal after whitespace canonicalisation. It failed with the class-level cluster rendering `identical` over inequivalent slices.
2. **Quarantined**: the fallback's comparison is deleted and replaced with the mandated `panic!` (`report_render.rs`, `csharp_method_declarations_are_equivalent`), so any C# scan that would have taken the defective path dies loudly instead of emitting the false label.
3. Left red, as the rule requires.

## Collateral (expected, mandated)

Every C# scan that reaches the fallback now panics, so these suites are red until the arm is rebuilt soundly:

- `csharp_identical_overclaim` (the pin)
- `csharp_issue_66_route_mapping`
- `csharp_type1_type2_distinct_buckets`
- `csharp_unrelated_xunit_classes` (2 tests)

The jellyfin corpus scan also panics, so the jellyfin gate cannot run until this is fixed.

## Sound replacement sketch (not applied — quarantine only)

The upgrade's evidence must cover **every** member the range contains, not just methods: compare the full canonicalised slices minus only the wrapper tokens the fallback was built to tolerate (class/namespace headers and using directives), or equivalently require that all *named members* in range — not just `method_declaration`s — are pairwise equivalent and that no member is unmatched. The original motivation (issue #66-era wrapper tolerance) must be re-verified against `csharp_identical_overclaim` before any re-land.

Found while curating the jellyfin corpus manifest for the corpus-assertion plan (section F); discovered because hand-diffing a mined `identical` cluster's byte ranges was NOT empty.

\`crates/deslop-lsp/tests/dependency_reactivity.rs\` (main, ~line 108–120): the assertion reads a count out of the notification JSON as

    .as_u64().unwrap_or_default() < 4

If the field is renamed, absent, or the notification shape changes, \`unwrap_or_default()\` yields \`0\`, \`0 < 4\` holds, and the test passes without having observed the behaviour it exists to bound. Fail-open: the reactivity regression it guards could return undetected.

## Fix shape

A missing field must fail the test, not default: \`ok_or\`/\`expect\` with a message naming the field, and assert the positive expected value (or exact range) rather than only an upper bound against a defaulted zero.

Found during the #364 branch audit; verified present on \`origin/main\` (\`unwrap_or_default\` at line 114).

title: fused_score_bounds.rs is fail-open: a report missing clusters/signals/fused passes the bound check vacuously
body:
## Defect (on main)

\`crates/deslop/tests/fused_score_bounds.rs\` (main, ~lines 27–52): the helper \`first_unbounded_fused\` walks the report with \`?\` at every step —

    let clusters = report.get("clusters")?.as_array()?;
    ... .get("signals")?.get("fused")? ...

and the caller treats \`None\` as "no unbounded fused score found" → **pass**. So a schema rename, a serialisation bug that drops \`signals\`, or an empty \`clusters\` array all make the bounds test pass while asserting nothing. The test would stay green if the detector went blind — exactly the class of assertion the testing rules ban.

## Fix shape

The helper must distinguish "every fused score is in bounds" from "I found no fused scores to check": assert a positive minimum cluster/signal count for the fixture first, and make a missing field a hard failure (\`ok_or\`/\`expect\` with a message), never a silent \`None\`.

Found during the #364 branch audit; verified present on \`origin/main\`.

## Relation

- #412 is the mechanism that hid it (substring skip).
- #166 is the underlying single-threaded / whole-corpus-in-RAM cost this ceiling was bounding.

## Fix shape

Either the performance regression is fixed until the run is back under its ceilings, or the ceilings are consciously re-measured and raised in a reviewed change with the regression tracked — never silently. The test must actually run somewhere in CI (see #412) for either to mean anything.

title: deslop-lsp writes no startup log when stderr is a pipe — which is what every real LSP client gives it
body:
## Measured

`deslop-lsp` emits its startup log to stderr when stderr is a **regular file**, and emits **nothing** when
stderr is a **pipe**. Same binary, same flags, same workspace, reproduced outside cargo:

```sh
WS=$(mktemp -d); ERR=$(mktemp)
# stderr -> FILE, stdin held open
( sleep 10 ) | RUST_LOG=info NO_COLOR=1 ./target/debug/deslop-lsp "$WS" --worker-threads 2 >/dev/null 2>"$ERR" &
sleep 5; wc -c < "$ERR"
#   2662
#   2026-...  INFO deslop_lsp::app: deslop-lsp args parsed ... worker_threads=2 ...
```

```sh
WS=$(mktemp -d); OUT=$(mktemp)
# stderr -> PIPE, stdin held open, stdout piped and unread — exactly what an LSP client does
( sleep 8 ) | RUST_LOG=info NO_COLOR=1 ./target/debug/deslop-lsp "$WS" --worker-threads 2 2>&1 >/dev/null | cat > "$OUT" &
sleep 6; wc -c < "$OUT"
#   0
```

With stdin at EOF (`< /dev/null`) the process shuts down promptly and the full log appears in both cases, so
the output is produced — it just does not reach a pipe while the server is running.

## Why it matters

A language server is always spawned with piped stdio. VS Code, the JetBrains plugin, and
`crates/deslop-lsp/tests/common` all give it a pipe. So in **actual production use** the startup log never
appears while the server runs.

`crates/deslop-lsp/tests/cpu_throttle_knob.rs` documents the user-facing contract it breaks:

> the startup log line records the chosen value so the user can confirm the knob took effect **by tailing
> the log**

You cannot tail a log that a pipe never receives. CLAUDE.md also requires logging entry and exit of
significant operations; that observability is absent on the transport every client uses.

## Consequence in the test suite

`deslop-lsp::cpu_throttle_knob::lsp_startup_log_records_the_worker_threads_knob` is **red and not
`#[ignore]`d**, so it is in the `make test` gate. It asserts `stderr` contains `worker_threads=2` and
observes zero bytes. Diagnostic added while investigating: the child is still alive (`early_exit=None`) after
20 s with an empty stderr, so this is not a spawn failure or an early crash.

The same test previously slept a flat 1500 ms, killed the child, and scraped `wait_with_output`, which made
it a race rather than a wait — it passed and failed on identical back-to-back runs. That has been replaced
with an event-driven read bounded by a 20 s deadline (and the banned `#[allow(unused_mut)]` removed), so the
test now fails for the real reason instead of intermittently.

## Suspected mechanism

Not investigated to root cause. The output appears on a file descriptor that is a regular file but not on a
pipe, which points at the log-destination selection rather than at buffering — a `BufWriter` would withhold
from a file too, and it does not. `docs/specs/cli.md` describes a `log → <file>` vs `log → stderr
(--log-to-console)` split; whatever chooses between them appears to treat a piped stderr as "not a log
destination".

Related: #370 (the undrained-stderr deadlock in the shared LSP test harness).

title: Rename anchor mass overshoots on short subtrees: a certified-perfect bijection caps at 0.667
body:
## Measurement request, not a threshold change

`RENAME_EVIDENCE_HALF_MASS = 4.0` discounts rename evidence by sample size:
`anchor_weight(n) = n / (n + 4.0)`. On a short subtree that caps a **perfect** rename proof below the
promotion floor.

## The case

`crates/deslop/tests/fixtures/ts-qualified-type-rename/`, restored to its pre-#341 maximal rename:

```ts
// alpha.ts (unchanged by #341)
export function formatLocal(clock: Intl.DateTimeFormat, value: number): string {
  const scaled = value * 2;
  return clock.format(scaled);
}
// beta.ts (maximal, pre-#341)
export function formatZoned(stamp: Temporal.Instant, amount: number): string {
  const scaled = amount * 2;
  return stamp.format(scaled);
}
```

Every difference is an identifier substitution: `formatLocal→formatZoned`, `clock→stamp` (2 occurrences),
`Intl→Temporal`, `DateTimeFormat→Instant`, `value→amount` (2 occurrences). The multiplier is `2` on both
sides. No differing literal, constant, control flow, arity or statement.

## Measured

```
bucket=structural_only  fused=0.6000  agreement=0.3636  rename_consistency=0.6667
structural=1.00  token_jaccard=1.00
```

Stable across `--min-nodes` 4/6/8/10/12/15/20 — not a min-nodes artifact.

Decomposed against `content.rs`, reproducing to the digit:

```
collapsed leaves = 10 identifier positions + 1 literal (`2`)
agreement            = (3 identity + 1 literal) / 11 = 0.3636
coverage             = 7/7   = 1.0
literal_preservation = 1/1   = 1.0
anchors              = 1 preserved literal + 7 explained = 8
anchor_weight(8)     = 8 / (8 + 4.0) = 0.6667
rename_consistency   = min(1.0, 1.0) * 0.6667 = 0.6667
```

**The engine's own `coverage = 1.0` and `literal_preservation = 1.0` certify the rename is total, bijective,
contradiction-free and literal-preserving.** It does not disbelieve the rename. It discounts it purely on
sample size, and misses `CONTENT_SUPPORT_FLOOR` (0.7) by **0.033**.

Confirming the mass term is the only variable: extending the same rename by two more corroborated statements
(anchors 8 → 14) gives `rename = 0.7778`, `fused = 0.700`, promoting. Identical clone-ness, different verdict,
body length the only difference.

## The discriminator is otherwise working — controls

- Genuinely unrelated same-shape pair (`formatLocal`/`priceLine`, `* 2` vs `* 3`, `.format` vs `.render`):
  `rename = 0.000`, `agreement = 0.000`, `fused = 0.000`. Correctly annihilated.
- The same maximal rename plus one behavioural literal change (`* 2` → `* 3`): `rename` collapses
  `0.667 → 0.000`, `fused` to 0.273.

So this is not the gate being appropriately strict; it is the mass term overshooting on a 30-node subtree.

## What is being asked for

**Do not just lower the constant.** What is needed first is a corpus sweep of what a length-relative mass
would admit — 8 anchors over 30 nodes is genuinely thin evidence, and this is the highest precision-risk of
the rename-evidence fixes. File the measurement, then decide.

Related: #405 (which introduced the smooth anchor mass and works correctly at larger sizes), #344, #409.

title: literal_preservation is a blind count — it manufactures false negatives AND tolerates a false positive
body: ## The defect `crates/deslop-core/src/content.rs:321`: ```rust literal_preservation(&literals).min(mapping.coverage) * anchor_weight(anchors) ``` `literal_preservation` is a **bare count** of how many literal positions are byte-identical. It never asks *why* a literal differs. So it treats these as the same evidence: - `"OrderService"` → `"UserService"` — a label renamed alongside the very symbol it names, i.e. part of the same consistent renaming the engine is trying to prove; - `* 0.9` → `* 0.75` — a changed discount rate, i.e. genuinely different behaviour. Both merely decrement a numerator. The verdict then turns on how many *other* literals happen to sit in the same subtree. ## Measured, both directions ### It manufactures false negatives `ts-decorators` (`crates/deslop/tests/fixtures/ts-decorators/`), restored to its pre-#341 maximal rename: a total identifier bijection across two controller classes. Demoted at `rename_consistency = 0.5467`, `fused = 0.5227`, `structural_only`. Harmonising **only the two string literals** — `"/orders"`→`"/users"` and `"OrderService"`→`"UserService"`, which are the same substitutions the engine already credits at the identifier leaves — moves it to `rename_consistency = 0.9149`, `fused = 0.8234`, `nearly_identical`. Two string literals move `rename_consistency` by **0.368** while moving `agreement` by 0.045. `ts-enums`: same mechanism. Harmonising the three renamed label strings takes `rename 0.5507 → 0.8462`, `fused 0.4957 → 0.7615`, promoting. `jsx-entity-invariance`: the only non-rename difference is `plus` vs `&` — **the exact invariance the fixture exists to prove**. Harmonising it takes `rename 0.3889 → 0.7895`. A fixture named `jsx-entity-invariance` is demoted because of the entity. Symptom worth noting: `rename_consistency` is **bit-identical** (0.5467, 0.3889) for the maximal and the softened version of those two families — a signal returning the same number for a 3-position and a 21-position diff is not measuring what its name says. ### It tolerates a false positive Same fixture family (`ts-comment-literal-invariance`), varying only which literals differ, min-nodes 12: | variant | differing literals | bucket | fused | rename | |---|---|---|---|---| | maximal | 4 of 6 | `structural_only` | 0.2314 | 0.2571 | | numerics harmonised | 2 of 6 | `structural_only` | 0.4653 | 0.5170 | | strings harmonised | 2 of 6 | `structural_only` | 0.5831 | 0.6478 | | **only the discount differs (`0.9` vs `0.75`)** | 1 of 6 | **`nearly_identical`** | **0.7013** | 0.7792 | | all harmonised (pure 13-name rename) | 0 of 6 | `nearly_identical` | 0.8200 | 0.9111 | **Row 4 is a false positive**: a changed discount rate — different business logic — is promoted to the act-now bucket because enough *other* literals happened to be preserved. So the demotion of the maximal pair is not the engine applying a behavioural principle; it is arithmetic on a count. ## What the fix must do (and must not break) Running literals through the same Baker modal-bijection / corroboration test as identifiers fixes `ts-decorators`, `ts-enums` and `jsx-entity-invariance` — **and also rescues the `0.9` vs `0.75` case**, which is precisely the precision case the gate exists for. So the fix has to distinguish *a label renamed alongside its subject* from *a changed numeric constant*. It must be re-measured against `dart_issue_197_single_file_structural_only.rs` and the F# data-table corpus before landing. ## Explicitly not a quarantine candidate The accuracy rule's `panic!` quarantine needs a scoped defect. `literal_preservation` is load-bearing precision machinery — it is what keeps the #197 endpoint-literal family and the F# data tables out of the act-now band. Measured: the #197 fixture already renders three visible `nearly_identical` clusters (`fused` 0.889 / 1.0 / 1.0) carried by `agreement` with `rename_consistency` at 0.31–0.50. Removing the literal term would raise those, not lower them. The defect is the *blindness* of the count, not the term's existence. Related: #405 (the anchor-mass repair, which works — a maximal 13-identifier rename over 115 nodes promotes at `rename 0.9111` provided literals are preserved), #344, #408.

title: False negative: a genuine Type-4 clone (recursive vs iterative sum) is dropped by MIN_COSINE — release gate now red
body:
## What is wrong

`crates/deslop/tests/fixtures/dart-issue-119-same-role/` holds a textbook Type-4 semantic clone:

```dart
int totalRecursive(int limit) {
  if (limit <= 0) { return 0; }
  return limit + totalRecursive(limit - 1);
}

int totalIterative(int limit) {
  var running = 0; var index = 1;
  while (index <= limit) { running = running + index; index = index + 1; }
  return running;
}
```

Both sum `1..limit`. Different code, identical behaviour — exactly what the semantic axis exists to find. **It does not surface.** No embedding pair forms, so no cluster is built and nothing is reported.

`deslop::dart_issue_119_embedding_role_mismatch::dart_same_role_function_pair_still_surfaces` is **red and is NOT `#[ignore]`d**, so `make ci` fails today.

## Why it only appeared now

It was never detected. It only *looked* detected.

The pre-#369 `MockOllama::embed_vector` returned `vec![len.sin(), first.cos(), 0.5, -0.5]`. The two constant lanes alone floor the cosine of any two vectors near 1.0, so every pair cleared the gate regardless of content. Commit `31d5efd18` replaced that with an honest signed shingle-hash signature (GH #366/#369), and the fixture immediately stopped pairing.

This is not a regression introduced by that commit — the commit made the instrument honest and the pre-existing recall hole became visible.

## Measured against the real embedder

Measured with live Ollama / `nomic-embed-text` (not the mock), against `MIN_COSINE = 0.80` at `crates/deslop-core/src/embedding/pairs.rs:21`:

| pair | honest mock | real embedder | gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| same-role (this fixture) | 0.2704 | **0.7763** | 0.80 |
| role-mismatch fixture | 0.0990 | 0.6101 | 0.80 |
| same-role + shared docstring | 0.5727 | 0.8311 | 0.80 |

**Production misses it too, by 0.037 of cosine.** This is a real false negative in the shipped product, not a test-harness artifact.

## What must NOT be done

Do not lower `MIN_COSINE` to turn the test green. Per CLAUDE.md, widening a threshold to make an assertion pass is prohibited, and 0.80 was not chosen against this evidence. Do not weaken or `#[ignore]` the assertion either — it is red for a true reason and pins a real defect.

## The second problem this exposes

`MockOllama` **structurally cannot represent a Type-4 clone**. Its signature is lexical (hashed byte shingles), so:

- a pair the real embedder considers semantically close (0.8311) the mock scores 0.5727 and drops;
- a pair lexically close enough for the mock to clear 0.80 is near-verbatim and routes to `identical` / `nearly_identical`, never `same_behavior`.

So no trustworthy `same_behavior` assertion can be driven through the mock at all. Either these fixtures move behind the real-Ollama gate (renamed `ollama_*`), or `MockOllama` gains a deterministic semantic-similarity mode. That is a harness decision with test-semantics consequences.

Related: #366 (mock measured length residues), #369, #358.

title: Corpus precision check matches raw source text: check_boilerplate_not_ranked_first is unsound in both directions
body:
## The defect

[`crates/deslop/tests/corpus_repos.rs:320`](https://github.com/Nimblesite/Deslop/blob/main/crates/deslop/tests/corpus_repos.rs#L320) matches `forbidden_top_shapes` against **raw source text**:

```rust
let text = first_occurrence_text(root, cluster)?;
for shape in &forbidden {
    if text.contains(shape) {
```

`CLAUDE.md` prohibits this outright — *"No using text pattern matching on source code or structured data. No RegEx on code. USE THE AST!"* — and the check is unsound in **both** directions.

### False positive in the gate

The string matches inside a comment, doc comment, or string literal. A legitimate cluster of genuine copy-paste that merely *mentions* `extends StatefulWidget` — in a doc comment, an error message, a test fixture string — is reported as un-deduplicable boilerplate. The gate fails a report that was correct.

### False negative in the gate

A declaration written `extends  StatefulWidget` (two spaces), or wrapped across a line, is not matched. The framework boilerplate the check exists to catch ranks #1 and walks straight past. The gate passes a report that was wrong.

## Why this matters beyond the check itself

This is `check_boilerplate_not_ranked_first` — the real-repository confirmation behind **#331** and **#336**.

**#331 was closed against it.** Its closure evidence is therefore produced by an instrument that can answer wrong in either direction, so the closure is not currently supported by a sound assertion.

`must_not_rank_first` is also the *only* curated precision surface the corpus gate has. Ranking is the product, and the head of the report is where a false positive does the most damage — so the one place precision is asserted on a real repository is asserted by string matching.

## Fix

- [ ] Failing test pinning both directions — a comment-only mention must **not** fire, a whitespace variant **must**. Watch it fail for the real reason.
- [ ] Quarantine the text-matching arm with the mandated `panic!` per the strict accuracy rule in `CLAUDE.md`, commented with what it did, why it was deleted, and which test pins it.
- [ ] Replace with a tree-sitter predicate over the occurrence's AST — a node-kind / supertype match, never a string. A superclass clause is a node, not a substring.
- [ ] Re-verify **#331** against the replacement, and **reopen it if the evidence does not survive**.
- [ ] Restate `forbidden_top_shapes` in `corpus/flutter.json` as AST predicates rather than source fragments, and specify the new form under [CORPUS-PRECISION] in `docs/specs/corpus.md`.

## Context

Tracked as section C of [`docs/plans/fused-score-followups.md`](https://github.com/Nimblesite/Deslop/blob/main/docs/plans/fused-score-followups.md), where it is sequenced **first** — ahead of the curated-precision surface and the per-repository curation — because it decides whether the existing precision evidence can be trusted at all.

Found while auditing what the corpus gate actually asserts after #347 made it boot. Related finding from the same audit: five of nine corpus repositories assert nothing beyond resource ceilings, and no manifest field can express "these two things are not duplicates".

title: ReportFixture forks one path into several FileIds, so same-file clusters test as cross-file
body:
## Defect

`ReportFixture` forks one source path into several `FileId`s, so any cluster whose members share a path is presented to the production router as **cross-file**. Every cross-file predicate downstream reads it wrong.

`FileRegistry::register` appends unconditionally — it has no path lookup:

```rust
pub fn register(&mut self, path: PathBuf) -> FileId {
    let index = u32::try_from(self.paths.len()).unwrap_or(u32::MAX);
    self.paths.push(path);
    FileId(index)
}
```

`ReportFixture::file` documents this hazard in its own doc comment:

> `FileRegistry::register` appends unconditionally, so registering per member would fork the same path into divergent ids.

…and then `ReportFixture::cluster` does exactly that — one `member()` call per snippet, each of which calls `file()`:

```rust
let members = snippets
    .into_iter()
    .enumerate()
    .map(|(index, (path, source))| self.member(path, source, node_count, index))
    .collect::<Vec<_>>();
```

## Reproduction

`crates/deslop-core/tests/issue_98_99_108_120_122_thresholds.rs` builds the GH #108 cluster from two snippets **both at `schemas.py`**:

```rust
("schemas.py", "def schema_report_get():\n    return {...}\n"),
("schemas.py", "def schema_top_offenders():\n    return {...}\n"),
```

Two functions in one module — but the fixture hands `report_bucket_kind` two distinct `FileId`s, so `members.iter().any(|m| m.file_id != first.file_id)` is true and the cluster looks like it spans two files. It is the only fixture in `crates/deslop-core/tests` that repeats a path, which is why this has stayed invisible.

## Why it matters

`report_render` routes on file spread in several places — `is_cross_file_scaffolding` (#134's 3-member/3-file rule) and `route_anchor_free`'s cross-file spread rule ([CLONE-BUCKETS-ROUTING] row 4, #396). A fixture that misreports spread can only test those rules against a corpus shape that cannot occur in the real pipeline, where two occurrences in one file necessarily share a `FileId`.

Today the #108 assertion passes for an unrelated reason — `route_anchor_free`'s *unmeasured* rule catches it, since `ReportFixture::cluster` stamps `ContentEvidence::unmeasured()`. So the spread lie is currently latent. It stops being latent the moment that rule is narrowed, and it will fail in the confusing direction: a same-file cluster silently routed by a cross-file rule.

## Suggested fix

Give `ReportFixture` a `path -> FileId` map so repeated paths resolve to one file, and have `member()` append its snippet to that file's source and point the member's `ByteRange` at the appended segment — modelling two occurrences in one file, which is what the paths already claim. No assertion needs to change.

title: Drive repo duplication from 13.65% back to 12.5% — clusters the C#-only row-4 carve-out was hiding
body:
## Context

[CLONE-BUCKETS-ROUTING] row 4 (`structural ≤ 0.01 ∧ token_jaccard ≥ 0.90 → nearly_identical`) was implemented for C# only, via a carve-out in `report_render`. Every other language's LSH-only Type-3 clone fell to `loosely_similar`, which the renderer hides — so real duplication in this repo's own Rust, TypeScript, Python and Dart measured as **zero** (gh #390).

Row 4 now routes in every language (PR #396). Measured with the corrected binary against both trees, so the comparison isolates code from detector:

| tree | duplication | redundant LOC | clusters |
|---|---|---|---|
| `main` @ 5813c795c | 13.9514% | 13504 | 876 |
| PR #396 | 13.6160% | 14052 | 913 |

The gate threshold was re-justified 12.5 → 13.65 in `.deslop.toml`, with the full rationale in the comment there. **Nothing was duplicated to cause the rise** — it was always there, and the gate could not see it.

## The work

Remove the ~1.1 points between 13.65 and 12.5. It is real DRY work, concentrated in files PR #396 does not touch:

- `crates/deslop-mcp/tests/cli.rs` — 591 redundant LOC, the single largest offender
- `clients/vscode/src/test/unit/` — ~1.1k LOC across `tree.topOffenders`, `command-impls`, `live-bubble`, `live-bubble-journey`, `extension-internals`
- `crates/deslop/tests/defaults.rs` — 310
- `crates/deslop-core/tests/refactor_consolidate.rs` — 292
- `crates/deslop/tests/cli/config.rs` — 237
- `crates/deslop-core/tests/live.rs` — 231

## The one thing this must not be

Lowering row 4 back to a C#-only carve-out, or otherwise widening a threshold to hide the clusters. That restores a confirmed false negative — a fully duplicated pair reporting zero duplication in every language but one. Ratchet `max_duplication_percent` down as the dedup lands, never by re-hiding.

Extracting shared helpers must not weaken any assertion: per CLAUDE.md, reducing assertiveness is prohibited.

title: RA-06: Win32 path semantics for the VS Code user-data dir are never exercised on Windows
body:
Split out of the `worktree-fused-score-followups` regression audit (RA-06, P2).

The POSIX socket-path cap and the Windows no-cap rule in `clients/vscode/scripts/vscode-test-user-data-dir.mjs` are correct, and 23 script tests run through the Ubuntu `make lint` job. But the injected `win32` case calls the host `node:path`, so on POSIX it never exercises Windows separators or native `%TEMP%` behaviour. The existing Windows CI job sets up Node and then runs only Rust checks and the TCP E2E.

The Windows path rule is therefore asserted by a test that cannot observe Windows path behaviour.

Fix:
- use `path.win32` when the injected platform is `win32`, so the unit semantics are host-independent
- run `node --test clients/vscode/scripts/*.test.mjs` in the Windows CI job

title: [CLONE-NOISE-RUST-LANGPARSER] filter is dead on main: stale 4-method trait-surface equality
body:
`[CLONE-NOISE-RUST-LANGPARSER]` cannot fire on `main`: the filter tests set **equality** against a hard-coded 4-method trait surface that no plug-in has matched since `LanguageParser` grew.

## The defect

`crates/deslop-core/src/cluster_filters/rust.rs:137-144` (on `main`):

```rust
fn language_parser_method_names() -> BTreeSet<Vec<u8>> {
    BTreeSet::from([
        b"id".to_vec(),
        b"file_extensions".to_vec(),
        b"grammar".to_vec(),
        b"parse_and_normalize".to_vec(),
    ])
}
```

`crates/deslop-core/src/cluster_filters/rust.rs:44-49` requires every member's impl to declare **exactly** that set:

```rust
let expected_methods = language_parser_method_names();
first.trait_name == b"LanguageParser"
    && first.methods == expected_methods
    && shapes
        .iter()
        .all(|shape| shape.trait_name == first.trait_name && shape.methods == expected_methods)
```

## Why it can never hold

`LanguageParser` has grown well past those four methods, and each first-party plug-in overrides a different subset. Method counts inside `impl LanguageParser for …` on `main`:

| Plug-in | Methods overridden |
|---|---|
| `crates/deslop-core/src/lang/csharp.rs` | 11 |
| `crates/deslop-core/src/lang/rust_lang.rs` | 11 |
| `crates/deslop-core/src/lang/dart.rs` | 10 |
| `crates/deslop-core/src/lang/python.rs` | 8 |

`python.rs` declares no `merge_tables` / `declared_type_of` / `emit_merge_method`; `dart.rs` declares no `emit_extract_method`. So `shape.methods == expected_methods` is false for **every** plug-in, and the two `all(...)` / equality conjuncts short-circuit the predicate to `false` on every input. `is_rust_language_parser_adapter_cluster` is dead code by construction.

`collect_rust_function_names` also recurses into method bodies, so any nested `fn` inside a method inflates `shape.methods` further — a second, independent way the equality drifts.

## Impact

Accuracy, false-positive direction. `[CLONE-NOISE-RUST-LANGPARSER]` exists to keep trait-contract adapter boilerplate out of the actionable tier. With the predicate permanently `false`, nothing suppresses that family — any clustering change that lets the adapter impls cluster surfaces them as `nearly_identical` business-logic duplication.

This is latent rather than currently visible on `main`: the adapter members are demoted by the routing tier instead, which masks the dead filter. `crates/deslop/tests/rust_trait_boilerplate_false_positive.rs` therefore passes on `main` **without exercising the filter at all** — it would still pass if `is_rust_language_parser_adapter_cluster` were deleted outright.

## Reproduction (observed)

On the `worktree-fused-score-followups` branch the sibling-window signature work changes member ranges, removing the routing demotion that masks this. `rust_language_parser_trait_impl_boilerplate_does_not_surface` then fails with the adapters surfaced as actionable:

```
bucket=Some("nearly_identical"), paths={"csharp.rs", "dart.rs", "python.rs", "rust_lang.rs"},
snippets=["csharp.rs: fn id(&self) -> &'static str {", "dart.rs: fn id(&self) -> &'static str {",
          "python.rs: fn id(&self) -> &'static str {", "rust_lang.rs: fn id(&self) -> &'static str {"]
```

## Fix

Two changes, both already made on `worktree-fused-score-followups`:

1. Replace the set-equality with a **subset** relation against the core surface (`id`, `file_extensions`, `grammar`, `parse_and_normalize`). A trait's method set grows over time and no impl overrides every default, so equality pins the filter to one historical trait revision and silently stops matching.
2. `rust_impl_shape_from_node` extracts the trait name by splitting raw bytes on `{` and string-matching `"impl "` / `" for "`. That is text pattern matching on source code, and it misreads generic parameters, `where` clauses, and paths such as `lang::LanguageParser`. Read `child_by_field_name("trait")` from the CST instead.

A regression test must pin the filter itself, not the routing tier — assert that the adapter cluster is absent for a reason that survives a routing change, so deleting the filter turns it red.

title: Dependabot SECURITY PRs to main skip CI, dependency review, and CodeQL — the only class the actor skip can fire on
body:
`ci.yml` and `codeql.yml` both short-circuit on the Dependabot actor:

```yaml
# ci.yml — classify step
if [ "$ACTOR" = "dependabot[bot]" ]; then
  echo "code=false"; echo "site=false"; exit 0
fi

# ci.yml — security (dependency-review) job
if: github.actor != 'dependabot[bot]'

# codeql.yml — analyze job
if: github.event.repository.visibility == 'public' && github.actor != 'dependabot[bot]'
```

Each carries the same justification: *"Dependabot PRs are swept into `dependabot-upgrades` and never merge to main directly, so the consolidation PR is where these run."*

**That justification does not apply to any PR these skips can actually fire on.**

Both workflows trigger on `pull_request: branches: [main]` only. Every Dependabot **version** update carries `target-branch: dependabot-upgrades` (`.github/dependabot.yml`, all four ecosystems), so those PRs never reach either workflow — there is nothing for the skip to save. The only Dependabot PR whose base is `main` is a **security** update, which GitHub opens against the default branch regardless of `target-branch`. And the sweep does not move it: `dependabot-automerge.yml` carries an explicit `BASE FILTER — dependabot-upgrades ONLY. Do not add main back.`

So the net effect is the inverse of the intent:

| Dependabot PR | Base | Skip fires? | Gated by CI / dep-review / CodeQL? |
|---|---|---|---|
| routine version bump | `dependabot-upgrades` | never (workflow not triggered) | no — by design, gated at consolidation |
| **security / CVE fix** | **`main`** | **always** | **no — and never will be** |

The one PR class opened *because of a known vulnerability* is the one class that merges to `main` with no build, no test suite, no dependency review, and no CodeQL scan. It shows all-green because every job either did not run or reported `skipped`, which branch protection counts as passing.

The dependency-review skip is the sharpest of the three: a CVE fix bump routinely pulls transitive dependencies the advisory said nothing about, and that job is the repo's only dependency vuln-gate (no cargo-deny, no osv-scanner).

## Expected

A Dependabot security PR against `main` gets the same validation as a human PR against `main`.

## Fix

Remove the three actor short-circuits. They cost nothing on the routine bumps they were written for, because those bumps never trigger these workflows.

Found during the regression audit of the `fused-score-followups` branch. That branch corrects a stale comment in `dependabot.yml` which claimed the sweep folded security PRs into staging and that dependency review still gated them — both untrue on `main`. The gate hole itself predates the branch.

title: ts-mixed-band: renamed copy `ledger_c` never surfaces, and three different-evidence clusters all render fused = 1.00
body:
`crates/deslop/tests/fixtures/ts-mixed-band` stages five TypeScript files: `ledger_a` (original), `ledger_d`/`ledger_e` (one parenthesis apart from it), `ledger_c` (a consistently renamed copy), and `ledger_b` (same shape, identifiers *and* every literal different).

A scan on `main` at `--min-nodes 15 --embeddings off` publishes three visible clusters and **`ledger_c` appears in none of them**:

```
nearly_identical nodes=353 s=1.00 t=1.00 e=0.00 fused=1.00  ledger_a, ledger_b, ledger_d
nearly_identical nodes=177 s=1.00 t=1.00 e=0.00 fused=1.00  ledger_a, ledger_b, ledger_d, ledger_e
structural_only  nodes=379 s=1.00 t=0.00 e=0.00 fused=0.00  ledger_a, ledger_b
```

## Two defects

**1. `ledger_c` is a false negative.** A consistently renamed copy of `ledger_a` is exactly the Type-2 clone the tool exists to find. It never surfaces, in any bucket, hidden or visible.

**2. The confidence axis carries no information across three genuinely different bands.** `ledger_b` differs from `ledger_a` in every identifier *and* every literal. `ledger_d` differs by one parenthesis. Both render `token_jaccard = 1.00, fused = 1.00` and land in the same cluster at the same confidence as a near-verbatim copy.

The mechanism for (2) is that `token_jaccard` is computed from the **normalised** kind stream, which is by construction the same stream the structural hash already matched on. `buckets.rs::content_gated_signals` then overwrites `token_jaccard` to `1.0` for any `NearlyIdentical` cluster with `structural >= 0.99`:

```rust
let token_jaccard = if kind == ClusterKind::NearlyIdentical && signals.structural >= 0.99 {
    1.0
} else {
    signals.token_jaccard
};
```

So on a shape-identical cluster the rendered `token_jaccard` is `1.0` unconditionally — it is not a measurement. The axis whose job is to catch what structural normalisation erased is reporting the erased representation back.

A side effect worth calling out separately: **no end-to-end assertion on a rendered `token_jaccard` can detect a token-layer regression** on a shape-identical cluster, because the renderer supplies the value. That includes the E2E coverage attached to #339. Token-layer regressions have to be pinned at the signature layer.

## Expected

- `ledger_c` surfaces as a clone of `ledger_a`.
- Clusters carrying visibly different content evidence do not all render `fused = 1.00`.

## Repro

```
deslop crates/deslop/tests/fixtures/ts-mixed-band --min-nodes 15 --embeddings off --no-incremental
```

Related: #339 (token signal from the fallback signature), #367 (ts-mixed-band recall under subsumption), #343 (fused saturation).

title: duplication_percent excludes generated code from the numerator but keeps it in the denominator
body:
`duplication_percent = 100 × duplicated_loc / analysed_loc`.

A file recognised as machine-generated has its occurrences flagged `hidden`, and hidden occurrences are excluded from `duplicated_loc`. Its lines stay in `analysed_loc`.

Numerator and denominator therefore describe different populations. Generated lines can only push the figure down — they are structurally incapable of contributing to the numerator. **Adding generated code to a repository lowers its reported duplication**, with no change to the hand-written code.

## Repro

Four F# files at `--min-nodes 10 --embeddings off --no-incremental`. `hand_A.fs` / `hand_B.fs` are a byte-identical hand-written pair. `wire_A.fs` / `wire_B.fs` are a byte-identical generated pair carrying `// <auto-generated />`, deliberately a different shape so the two families cannot cluster together. Every file is 10 LOC.

| corpus | `analysed_loc` | `duplicated_loc` | `duplication_percent` |
|---|---|---|---|
| hand-written pair only | 20 | 20 | **100.00%** |
| same pair + generated pair | 40 | 20 | **50.00%** |

`hand_A.fs` and `hand_B.fs` each report `duplicated_loc = 10` in both runs. Only the denominator moved.

The generated pair is genuinely duplicated code. Hiding it from the ranked report and counting it under `clusters_hidden` is correct. The defect is only that its lines remain in the denominator of a percentage whose numerator excludes them.

## Mechanism

| location | behaviour |
|---|---|
| `crates/deslop-core/src/config.rs:775` | `has_generated_header` — banner match over the first 1 KiB |
| `crates/deslop-core/src/report_render.rs:130` | occurrence flagged `hidden` when the banner matches |
| `crates/deslop-core/src/report_metrics.rs:245-256` | `occurrence_is_hidden` gates the numerator |
| `crates/deslop-core/src/report_metrics.rs:127` | `analysed_loc` sums every analysed file — no hidden filter |
| `crates/deslop-core/src/report_metrics.rs:143` | `percent(duplicated_loc, analysed_loc)` |

`docs/specs/pipeline.md` has the same gap. Of `duplicated_loc`:

> Hidden occurrences (`[EXCLUSION-CONFIG]` `report_hide`) are **excluded** so a noisy generated-code tier cannot inflate the metric.

Of `duplication_percent`:

> `100.0 × duplicated_loc / analysed_loc`

`analysed_loc` carries no corresponding exclusion, so the rule that protects the numerator has no counterpart in the denominator.

## Scale

On `dotnet/fsharp` @ `v15.2.302`, 214 files carry a recognised banner — 8,625 LOC of 934,677 analysed, about 0.92%, so the understatement there is small.

It is not small in general. The error is proportional to the generated share: a repository that is 40% generated understates by roughly 40% relative. Large protobuf, OpenAPI, EF-migration or lexer/parser output reaches that routinely.

## Why it matters

- `--fail-over` gates CI on this number, so the gate can be satisfied by adding generated code rather than by removing duplication.
- The figure measures no single population, so it is not the transparent, accurate calculation the accuracy bar requires.
- It is silent and one-directional: it always understates, and nothing in the report signals by how much.

## Options

1. Exclude hidden LOC from `analysed_loc` too. The percentage then means "duplication among the code a human wrote", and both halves describe one population. Moves every reported number — needs a spec change and new assertions.
2. Publish the second denominator alongside the current one (e.g. `analysed_loc_visible`) so consumers can compute either and the asymmetry is visible on the wire.
3. Promote generated code from `report_hide` to `exclude` so it is never parsed. Cheapest, but forfeits the "hand-written code duplicates a generated file" signal that `report_hide` exists to provide.

Option 1 with option 3 as opt-in config looks right.

title: [PIPELINE-INCREMENTAL] Analysis is not incremental: 78% of every run is LSH + pair evaluation, recomputed in full however little changed
body:
`deslop` re-does the overwhelming majority of its work on every invocation regardless of how much of the corpus changed. The incremental cache ([PIPELINE-INCREMENTAL]) covers the parse stage only, and the parse stage is under a tenth of a run.

The spec frames incremental analysis as the first-class path — *"the LSP runs on it permanently, and a batch CLI run is just 'incremental starting from an empty cache'"* (`docs/specs/pipeline.md` [PIPELINE-INCREMENTAL], Activation). In practice only parsing is incremental. Nothing downstream is, and the code says so plainly at `crates/deslop-core/src/pipeline/session/change.rs:29`:

> the whole LSH → embedding → pair → cluster → rank → render chain downstream of it

That chain re-runs in full when a single file changes.

## Measured

400-file / 2.9 MB Rust corpus, warm cache (400 hits / 0 misses), three consecutive runs, times from the stage log:

| stage | run 1 | run 2 | run 3 | share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| discovery | 16 ms | 18 ms | 18 ms | 0.5% |
| **parse + normalise + fingerprint** | **302 ms** | **326 ms** | **304 ms** | **~9%** |
| LSH + candidate pair evaluation | 2486 ms | 2618 ms | 2598 ms | **~78%** |
| cluster + rank | 23 ms | 13 ms | 13 ms | 0.5% |
| render | 7 ms | 12 ms | 7 ms | 0.3% |
| buckets + metrics | 317 ms | 314 ms | 338 ms | ~10% |
| write JSON | 69 ms | 88 ms | 84 ms | 2.5% |

The cached stage is the bolded one. Everything else recomputes unconditionally.

Corroborated by wall clock on the same corpus: `--no-incremental` 7.10 s, fully warm 6.39 s — a 10% saving, matching the 9% stage share. An earlier run on `crates/deslop-core/src` (125 files) gave the same ratio.

## Scale of the recomputation

That run produced 87,251 fingerprints and evaluated 59,410 candidate pairs, of which 5,960 survived. Change one file out of 400 and all 59,410 are generated and scored again.

Pair scoring itself is cheap — `estimate_jaccard` is 128 `u64` comparisons, so ~7.6 M comparisons total, which cannot account for 2.5 s. The cost is far more likely the per-fingerprint MinHash signatures: `Signature = [u64; 128]` (`crates/deslop-core/src/lsh.rs:37`), one blake3 XOF fill per k-gram, across 87,251 subtrees. That attribution is an inference from the shape of the numbers, not a measurement — the 2.5 s has not been broken down into signature / banding / scoring, and it needs to be before anyone designs against it.

## Consequences

- A large repository pays full analysis cost on every CI run and every editor save, however small the change.
- The LSP's incremental path is incremental in name only; `update_files` splices the corpus and then re-runs the same 78%.
- Persisting the cache across CI sessions (#381) inherits this ceiling: the most it can ever save is the ~9% parse share.
- The disk economics in #379 follow directly — the cache is attached to the one stage where caching is cheapest to implement and least valuable to have.

## Spec gap

There is no spec section describing incremental analysis beyond the fingerprint cache. [PIPELINE-INCREMENTAL] specifies the parse cache and its invalidation; [PIPELINE-DETERMINISM] establishes that identical corpus state yields identical candidate sets, scores and cluster ids — which is precisely the property any downstream reuse would rest on — but nothing states what an incremental pass is permitted to reuse, or what equivalence it must preserve against a cold run. That contract has to exist before an implementation can be reviewed against it.

## Related

- #379 — the disk cost of caching this stage.
- #381 — CI persistence, capped by this ceiling.
- Design work: [`docs/plans/incremental-analysis-plan.md`](../blob/main/docs/plans/incremental-analysis-plan.md)

title: [ACTION-METADATA] GitHub action never persists .deslop/cache: every Marketplace run is a cold parse
body:
`action.yml` never persists `.deslop/cache`. There is no `actions/cache` step, and no cache-related input — every Marketplace run of the action is a cold run, re-parsing the entire tree from scratch. The incremental cache ([PIPELINE-INCREMENTAL]) is default-on and already writes to disk; CI simply throws it away between runs.

## Proposal

Restore and save the cache dir around the analysis step, keyed so correctness cannot regress:

- Path is the **scan root**, not the repo root — `.deslop/cache` lands under the `path:` input, so the cache path must be derived from it.
- The key must include the resolved deslop version. Blobs are already partitioned by version on disk, so a stale restore is inert rather than wrong, but keying on it avoids dragging dead partitions around.
- An opt-out input, for repos that would rather pay the parse cost than carry the artifact.

## What this does and does not buy

Honest sizing, measured on `crates/deslop-core/src` (125 files, 1.1 MB): cold 0.86 s, warm 0.78 s — about **9%**. The fingerprint cache elides tree-sitter parsing only; clustering, LSH, fusion and ranking re-run in full every time and are cached nowhere. The win grows with corpus size and with embeddings enabled, where the separate embedding cache under the same directory is doing the expensive work.

Two blockers should land first or the CI cache actively hurts:

- #379 — nothing ever evicts. Restore-and-save means the cache never cold-starts, so it grows monotonically toward GitHub's 10 GB repository ceiling, at which point Actions starts evicting *other* entries in the repo.
- #382 — the per-file cache key is currently unsound and the code path is quarantined behind a `panic!`. Persisting a cache whose keys collide would carry the corruption between runs instead of confining it to one.

## Relationship to #364

This was proposed on #364 as an alternative to `--diff` / `--only-changed`. It is worth doing on its own merits, but it does not answer that request. The incremental cache stores `(normalised AST, fingerprints)` per file content — it is a **parse** cache, not a report cache. It makes a run faster; it retains nothing about what was reported last time, so it cannot say which clusters are new in a change. Diff-scoped reporting needs the diff's line ranges (as #364 proposes) or a persisted prior report plus a cluster handle that survives between runs — which is #349.

## Related

- #364 — diff-aware scanning; this is the idea raised there, tracked separately.
- #349 — stable cluster slug, required for any run-over-run report diffing.
- #379, #382 — must land first.

title: [PIPELINE-INCREMENTAL] Cache partition keys on CARGO_PKG_VERSION, which is 0.0.0-dev in every local build: normalisation changes never invalidate the cache
body:
`crates/deslop-core/src/fpcache.rs:38` pins the tool version into the cache directory path:

```rust
const TOOL_VERSION: &str = env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION");
```

with the stated contract:

> Tool version pinned into the cache key so a `deslop-core` bump (grammar pins, normalisation rules, hashing changes) invalidates every previously-cached blob.

The workspace version is `0.0.0-dev` (`Cargo.toml:13`). Release builds rewrite it via `scripts/stamp-release-version.mjs`, so **shipped** binaries partition correctly and a user upgrading deslop gets a clean cache. Every local build does not: `cargo build` always stamps `0.0.0-dev`, so every local revision of deslop — before and after any change to normalisation, fingerprinting, or a grammar pin — reads and writes the **same** cache partition.

Observed directly: `.deslop/cache/fingerprints/rust/0.0.0-dev/10/…`

## Consequence

Change how a language normalises, rebuild, re-run against a tree you already scanned, and every unchanged file is served its pre-change normalised tree and pre-change fingerprints. The run reports against the old normaliser for cached files and the new one for changed files, in the same report. Depending on which way the change cuts, that is a false negative (a clone the new rules would surface stays hidden) or a false positive (a cluster the new rules would reject is still reported) — and it is silent, because a hit is indistinguishable from correct output.

The blast radius is developer and agent workflow, not shipped binaries:

- Any accuracy fix in this repo is verified against a cache that predates it, unless the developer knows to `rm -rf .deslop/cache` first. Nothing in the tooling says so.
- `CLAUDE.md` mandates running Deslop on Deslop (`find-similar` before writing code, `top-offenders` for cleanup). Agents following that instruction after a normalisation change get stale answers and have no signal that anything is wrong.
- Grammar pins are dependencies, not workspace version bumps. A `tree-sitter-*` upgrade changes the AST while `CARGO_PKG_VERSION` stays put — so this is not purely a `0.0.0-dev` problem. Even between releases, the version is not a sound proxy for "everything that determines the cached bytes".

The doc comment describes an invariant that nothing enforces. A version string cannot express "the normaliser changed"; only something derived from the inputs that produce the blob can.

## Fix direction

Derive the partition from what actually determines the cached bytes — a build-time hash over the normalisation/fingerprinting surface and the resolved grammar versions — rather than from a package version that is constant across every local build and independent of the grammars.

## Related

- #382 — same file, same cache: the per-file key is also unsound.

title: [PIPELINE-INCREMENTAL] Fingerprint cache costs 119 MB on this repo to save 10% of run time, and never reclaims it
body:
The incremental fingerprint cache ([PIPELINE-INCREMENTAL]) functions correctly — every hit is a hit, and cached and uncached runs produce identical reports. It costs far more disk than it saves time, and the disk it takes is never given back.

## What it costs

`.deslop/cache` in this repository, today:

```
119 MB   2,438 files
  └─ fingerprints/    118 MB
  └─ live-report.json 820 KB
```

The Rust corpus it describes is **400 files, 2.9 MB**. The cache is roughly 40× the size of the source.

A single clean snapshot of those 400 files costs **16 MB**. The remaining 103 MB is accumulation.

## What it buys

Measured on a clean copy of the 400-file Rust corpus, same machine, back to back:

| run | wall clock | cache |
|---|---|---|
| `--no-incremental` | 7.10 s | none |
| cache on, populating | 7.06 s | 0 hits / 400 misses |
| cache on, warm | 6.39 s | 400 hits / 0 misses |

**0.71 s — about 10%.** An earlier measurement on `crates/deslop-core/src` (125 files, 1.1 MB → 5.4 MB of blobs) gave 0.86 s → 0.78 s, about 9%. Two corpora an order of magnitude apart, same ratio.

## Why the return is that low

The cache elides tree-sitter parse + normalise + fingerprint, and nothing else. Everything downstream re-runs in full on every invocation regardless of how many files changed — stated outright at `crates/deslop-core/src/pipeline/session/change.rs:29`:

> the whole LSH → embedding → pair → cluster → rank → render chain downstream of it

Parsing is ~10% of a run. The cache is attached to the pipeline's cheapest stage.

## Growth

No code path in `crates/deslop-core/src/fpcache.rs` or `crates/deslop-core/src/embedding/cache.rs` deletes anything — no eviction, no TTL, no size cap, no reconciliation against the live corpus. Blobs are keyed by content hash, so every version a file has ever had persists, and a deleted source file's blobs persist too.

Reproduced on three files with one line appended between runs: 3 blobs → 7 blobs over five edits. Observed on this repository: **1,973 Rust blobs for 400 Rust files**, dated 2026-08-02 through 2026-08-16 with nothing removed in between. Roughly five stored versions per file, i.e. two weeks of edit history.

Partitioning multiplies it. Blobs are namespaced by tool version, so each version carries a complete copy:

```
rust/0.0.0-dev/30/   662 blobs   34 MB
rust/0.30.0/30/      319 blobs   14 MB
rust/0.31.0/30/      992 blobs   52 MB
```

`0.0.0-dev` is every local build ever run — see #380, where that string never changes across local revisions.

## Where it hurts

- **Local checkouts** — 119 MB and climbing for the life of the clone. An LSP session re-analyses on every save, so a live workspace is the fastest-growing case.
- **CI under #381** — `actions/cache` restore-and-save never cold-starts, so growth is monotonic and unattended, heading for GitHub's 10 GB repository ceiling. Past that, Actions begins evicting other entries in the repo.

## Open questions for triage

Not a prescription — the shape of the answer depends on which of these is true:

- Is a 10% saving worth any disk cost, or should the subsystem be removed outright?
- If caching is worth keeping, is the parse stage the right thing to cache, given the other 90% re-runs? What would it take to cache cluster results instead?
- If it stays as-is, what reclaims the space, and on whose schedule?

Whatever the answer, it should be judged against the numbers above rather than against the assumption that a cache is inherently worth having.

## Related

- #381 — persisting this in CI is what makes the growth unattended.
- #380 — version partitioning, one of the two multipliers.
- #382 — separate accuracy defect in the same cache's key derivation.
